extracted.subtask_description: A wartime newspaper report summarizing U.S. State Department telegrams charging Japanese authorities with multiple violations of the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention and giving battlefield news. Focus is on documenting alleged mistreatment of American and Filipino prisoners and internees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge I — Denial of protecting-power access (Article 86)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives of the Swiss government entrusted with the protection of American interests in Japan and Japanese-occupied territory have not been permitted to go to every place without exception where prisoners of war and civilian internees are interned, have not been permitted to interview without witnesses the persons held, and have not had access to all places occupied by the prisoners (Article 86 of the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The telegram urges that the Swiss minister be asked to visit each place without exception and to report on steps taken by Japanese authorities to rectify conditions. Examples cited: many camps in the Philippines, Indo-China, Thailand, Manchuria, Burma, Malaya and the Dutch East Indies have never been visited by Swiss representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge II — Refusal of International Red Cross visits (Articles 79 and 88)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives of the International Red Cross Committee have been refused permission to visit most of the places where American nationals are held by the Japanese authorities (Articles 79 and 88).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government notes restricted or no access to many camps; by contrast U.S.-held camps have been repeatedly inspected by protecting powers and the Red Cross. The restriction of such visits is cited as a principal category of deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge III — Denial of ability to forward complaints (Article 42)
rubrics_metrics.description: American nationals have not been permitted to forward complaints to the Japanese holding authorities or to representatives of the protecting power (Article 42).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The telegram lists instances where prisoners were prevented from communicating complaints; it specifically notes 'communications denied permission to address the camp commander' as an example and stresses this denial as a violation of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge IV — Punishing prisoners for complaining (Article 42)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese authorities have punished and have threatened to punish American nationals for complaining concerning the conditions of captivity (Article 42).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cancellation of dental appointments and deprivation of meals as collective punishments; prisoners struck for asking for food or water. The government cites these practices as direct violations and calls for discipline of responsible officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge V — Failure to furnish needed clothing (Article 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government has failed to furnish needed clothing to American nationals (Article 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: civilian internees at Hong Kong went without footwear; civilian internees at Kobe suffered lack of warm clothing; prisoners forced to march clad only in loin clothes. The telegram links lack of clothing to suffering and disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge VI — Confiscation of personal effects (Article 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese authorities have confiscated personal effects from American civilian internees and prisoners of war (Article 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Japanese soldiers covered an arm or wrist with wrist watches stolen from Americans. Confiscation of essential articles (e.g., drinking canteens) during marches is cited as causing additional suffering and death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge VII — Subjecting prisoners to insults and public curiosity (Article 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: American prisoners and civilian internees have been subjected to insults and public curiosity (Article 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tours of internment camps by Japanese school children, soldiers and civilians were encouraged at Baguio, Hongkong and Tsingtao; prisoners were displayed for propaganda photos and films (e.g., forced to be photographed operating captured American equipment). Such treatment is cited as degrading and contrary to the Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge VIII — Deficiency diseases due to inadequate diet; failure to provide health-sustaining food (Article 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deficiency diseases such as beriberi, pellagra, scurvy, sprue are common throughout Japanese internment camps due to callous failure of the authorities to provide a health-sustaining diet (Article 11 and reciprocal undertakings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report gives the Davao penal colony example where prisoners could see citrus fruit they were not allowed to pluck; it argues that dependence solely on Japanese-provided rations caused widespread deficiency diseases and unnecessary deaths, and urges permitting supplemental shipments under neutral guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge IX — Improper use of canteen profits (Article 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese authorities have devoted to improper and forbidden uses the profits of the sale of goods in camp canteens instead of devoting them to the welfare of the persons held in the camps (Article 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: canteen profits not used for prisoners' benefit (Hongkong camps); the telegram treats this as a misuse of resources that should aid internees' welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge X — Compelling civilians to perform labor other than camp administration (Article 27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to Japan's undertaking, the detaining authorities have compelled civilians to perform labor other than that connected with the administration, maintenance and management of internment camps (Article 27).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: civilian internees at Baguio were forced to repair sawmill machinery without remuneration. The government stresses that civilians should not be forced into such labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XI — Forcing officers and non-commissioned officers into improper labor (Article 27 / Article 31)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officer prisoners of war have been forced to labor and non-commissioned officers to do other than supervisory labor; prisoners have been required to perform labor that has a direct relation with war operations (Articles 27 and 31).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ten American engineers forced to assist rebuilding military installations; prisoners worked in a machine-tool-shop at Mukden. The telegram condemns use of prisoners on war-related labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XII — Denial or inadequacy of medical care (Article 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical care has in many instances been denied to prisoners of war and civilian internees and when given has been generally so poor as to cause unnecessary suffering and unnecessary deaths (Article 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific example: deplorable conditions in Philippine camps such as San Fernando where overcrowding and lack of care led to widespread disease and death. The report calls for adequate medical care and supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XIII — Failure to report names of prisoners and dead (Article 17, and related provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government has reported the names of only a part of the American prisoners of war and civilian internees in its hands (Article 17) and of American combatants found dead (Article 4 of the convention for the amelioration of the sick and wounded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States cites lack of complete lists as preventing families and protecting powers from accounting for and assisting prisoners; accurate reporting of names is demanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XIV — Prohibition or restriction of free exercise of religion (Article 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government has not permitted internees and prisoners of war freely to exercise their religion (Article 16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The telegram notes restrictions on religious exercise and demands that detaining authorities permit free practice of religion in line with the Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XV — Failure to post the Convention in English translation (Article 84)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government has failed to post the convention in camps in English translation, thus depriving American prisoners of war and civilian internees of knowledge of their rights thereunder (Article 84).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting an English translation of the Convention in camps is cited as a basic obligation to inform detainees of their rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XVI — Inadequate equipment and accommodations; inhumane living conditions (Article 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government has failed to provide adequate equipment and accommodations in prisoner of war and civilian internment camps and transports, but on the contrary forced them to subsist in inhumane conditions (Article 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: extreme overcrowding and insanitary conditions at San Fernando and other camps; the telegram contrasts this with U.S. treatment of Japanese nationals, which it says meets Convention standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XVII — Failure to apply fair trial/punishment provisions; imposition of cruel punishments without trial (Title III, Section V, Chapter 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government has completely failed to apply the provisions of the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention with regard to trial and punishment of prisoners of war and has imposed cruel and inhuman punishments without trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report cites repeated violations where prisoners were punished without lawful trial; the U.S. demands implementation of legal safeguards and disciplinary action against offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charge XVIII — Infliction of corporal punishment and torture (Article 46); murder and extreme cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese authorities have inflicted corporal punishment and torture upon American nationals (Article 46); there are authenticated cases of brutal murder, beatings, water cure torture, decapitation and other atrocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific incidents cited: Lieutenant Colonels Lloyd Biggs and Howard Breitung and Lt. R. D. Gilbert were severely beaten, tied to posts, stripped and later killed (one by decapitation); Sgt. McFee was shot after seizing a canteen of water. The telegram demands that those responsible be tracked down and punished.
